A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 18 pages of v3 and 22 pages of v4, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures sufficient for reliable comparison.

before.justification: V3 reports original Monte Carlo simulations, Chatbot Arena analyses and distribution-shift experiments in Sections 7–8 and the appendices.

after.justification: V4 retains those results and adds multicategory simulations, empirical judge-positioning analyses, AlpacaEval results and ranking-recovery experiments.

M1.justification: Appendix B develops v3's prospective multinomial extension into an explicit, tested k-category estimator using an estimated confusion-matrix inverse. This extends the procedure's inputs and outputs, while the binary estimator, confidence-interval construction and adaptive allocation algorithm remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V4 adds AlpacaEval data for GPT-4 win-rate analysis and a synthetic six-category review-score distribution-estimation task. The review categories label simulated outcomes, not actual reviews. Existing Chatbot Arena coverage and binary simulation configurations are retained.

E2.justification: The distribution-shift comparison retains the naive, calibration-only, difference/PPI and conditional-calibration comparators. Added experiments continue comparing raw judgments with corrected estimates. Additional LLM judges supply alternative judge configurations, rather than new correction baselines.

E3.justification: V4 introduces seven-judge Chatbot Arena positioning and four-judge AlpacaEval protocols, plus a six-category simulation with 1,000 test and 200 calibration items. Appendix K adds Kendall's tau, exact-ranking recovery and a GPT-4.1 condition using a 60%/40% test/calibration split. The original binary simulations and 90%/10% Chatbot Arena protocol are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses locate measured judge characteristics within theoretical variance regimes and examine whether judgment bias distorts model rankings. Appendix K also tests calibration-budget sensitivity through the additional 40% calibration condition. Original allocation analyses, distribution-shift experiments and the appendix binary simulation grid are retained.

E5.justification: New Table 3 reports means and standard errors over 10 multicategory Monte Carlo repetitions. Existing confidence-interval reporting, 10,000 binary simulation replications and 100 random Chatbot Arena splits remain unchanged; the new repetition count does not indicate fewer runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 values and matched plots are retained. V4 adds category-count estimates, judge characteristics, additional bias results and ranking outcomes. Table 4 reports raw/corrected exact-ranking recovery of 0%/37% for Gemini-3-Flash, 86%/46% for GPT-4.1 with 10% calibration, and 61%/75% with 40% calibration. These are newly reported comparisons under distinct conditions, not improvements over v3 scores. Figure 20 displays five target models despite adjacent prose referring to six.

T1.justification: Proposition 6.1 and its appendix proof expand the variance comparison from equal sensitivity and specificity to asymmetric q0 and q1, deriving a generalized condition and admissible accuracy interval. Appendix B additionally formalizes multicategory labels, confusion-matrix estimation and the nonsingularity requirement. The original binary estimator and confidence-interval derivations remain.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central bias-correction, uncertainty, allocation and conditional robustness claims. The introduction makes a limited addition to the contribution list by explicitly promising empirical positioning of contemporary judges within the variance regimes.

C2.justification: V4 adds substantive discussion of human disagreement, task-dependent variance advantages and ranking deterioration caused by limited calibration. Appendix B discusses rare-category estimation difficulties. Appendix A expands the earlier nuisance-factor discussion, adds complementarity with judge debiasing and adaptation, and removes the conformal-prediction future direction. These changes substantially clarify applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: Added appendices document response-pair selection and positive-class encoding for judge positioning, multicategory calibration construction, and ground-truth ranking construction and split settings. The binary Python listing and stated repository access are retained, moving from Appendix C to Appendix F.

R1.justification: V4 adds the Li et al. (2023) AlpacaEval reference and discusses complementarity with judge-level debiasing and adaptation. Positioning relative to Rogan–Gladen correction, PPI and conditional calibration remains substantially unchanged. Other bibliography revisions mainly concern formatting and metadata.

P1.justification: V4 edits introductory prose, adjusts the ordering within Section 6, moves future work into Appendix A and reorganizes the appendices. Author affiliations and publication information also change. Most existing exposition and the main section sequence remain intact, so the added scientific material does not amount to wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: V4 adds judge-positioning Figures 6 and 11, asymmetric-regime Figure 9, the three-panel bias Figure 20, and Tables 3 and 4. Figure 1 gains sensitivity/specificity labels, while existing displays are resized, relocated or renumbered. This substantially expands the visual presentation; retained plots are not new results merely because they moved.

improvement.justification: V3's variance theorem covered symmetric judge errors and lacked empirical positioning of real judges. V4 generalizes that theorem and connects it to measured judge characteristics on two benchmarks. The ranking experiments expose calibration-induced losses as well as benefits, and expanded limitations make the guarantees more useful and better qualified. These are substantial improvements in theoretical applicability and evidential support, despite minor inconsistencies such as Appendix K's six-model prose accompanying five-model bias plots.
